> 昔之得一者：天得一以清，地得一以寧，神得一以靈，谷得一以盈.

Chapter 38 drew the sliding: lose the way, then 德, then 仁, then 義, then 禮. Chapter 39 looks at the bottom of that slide and finds something still holding it up.

Six 得一, six 無以, and then a turn toward the lowest position of all — 孤, 寡, 不穀.

## 得一

一 is not 壹. The old distinction matters: 壹 is a sealed, counted unit; 一 is the undivided. 得一 is not "getting one thing" — it is holding the undivided.

天得一以清 — heaven holds the one and is clear. Not "heaven is clear because it has one"; rather, heaven's clarity is what its holding produces.

神得一以靈 — 神 here is the 引 that brings things out, the generative potential from chapter 6. 靈 is its efficacy: the thing works because it is undivided, not because it is powerful.

谷得一以盈 — the valley holds the one and is filled. The low place is full precisely because it does not compete for the fill.

## 其致之

> 其致之：天無以清，將恐裂.

Push it to the end: heaven without that clarity will, one fears, crack.

Note the six verbs — 裂, 廢, 歇, 竭, 滅, 蹶. Each is a specific failure of a specific thing, and each is the loss of what holding the one was producing.

蹶 is to fall straight down, to topple — the fall of a thing whose legs have gone out.

## The turn to the bottom

> 故貴以賤為本，高以下為基.

The noble takes the lowly as its root; the high takes the low as its foundation.

This is the same geometry as chapters 8, 28, and 32: the position that holds everything sits lower than what it holds. Here it is stated as construction: a foundation is not a lesser part of the building; it is what the building stands on, and it is always underneath.

## 孤、寡、不穀

> 是以侯王自稱孤、寡、不穀.

The rulers call themselves 孤 — orphan; 寡 — the one with few; 不穀 — the one not worthy of being fed.

These are the terms of the lowest position, used by the highest. The chapter asks: 此非以賤為本邪？非乎？ — is this not taking the lowly as the root? Is it not?

Note the double question. The first asks; the second presses. Laozi is not certain the rulers mean it — the form is right, and the sincerity is in question.

## 致數輿無輿

> 故致數輿無輿.

Count the parts of a carriage and you get no carriage.

The usual reading is "take the cart apart and count the pieces and you no longer have a cart," which is true and too easy. 輿 is not the wheels or the shafts — it is the carriage box.

The box is hollow. Count the wheels, the axles, the shafts, and you will never count the empty place. Which is the point of the chapter: the thing that carries is not among the things that can be counted.

## 琭琭如玉，珞珞如石

> 不欲琭琭如玉，珞珞如石.

Not wanting to be lustrous like jade, nor rough like stone.

Both are extremes of the same error: jade is precious and rare, stone is coarse and common, and each is a fixed position in a ranking. The chapter declines both — not to become neither, but to stop being classifiable.
